questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: "She ___ play the piano very well."
questions.explanation: "Can" + base verb expresses ability, and it is the same for every subject: she can play. A modal never takes -s ("cans"), never takes "to" ("can to") and never comes after "is".

questions.prompt: Choose the best advice: "Your room is very untidy. You ___ tidy it before your cousins arrive."
questions.explanation: "Should" + base verb gives advice, a good thing to do: you should tidy it. "should to" wrongly adds "to", "mustn't" forbids tidying the room, and "had to" is a past obligation, not advice.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Students ___ wear a uniform at school. It is the rule."
questions.explanation: A rule is an obligation, something necessary with no choice, so "have to" (or "must") fits: students have to wear a uniform. "should" is only advice, "might" is a possibility, and "is able to" expresses ability and does not agree with "students".

options.text: You are able to swim here.

questions.explanation: "Mustn't" + base verb expresses prohibition: you mustn't smoke here, you have no right to do it. "should" gives advice, "might" says something is possible, and "are able to" says what you can do.

"Be able to" + base verb expresses ability, with "be" agreeing with the subject: he is able to read. "able" always keeps its "to", "be" cannot disappear, and the verb after "to" stays bare, so "reads" is wrong.

questions.prompt: Complete: "I'm not sure, but she ___ be at the library."
questions.explanation: "I'm not sure" means perhaps, and "might" + base verb says that something is possible: she might be at the library. "should" gives advice, "had to" is a past obligation and "mustn't" is a prohibition.
